evals.prompt: I have newspaper-readership data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/newspaper.parquet for 580 readers — Income (High/Low) and Newspaper (USA Today / WS Journal). I want to test whether income level and newspaper choice are associated. Walk me through it.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py (or its Python equivalent) to load the parquet, finds and reads newspaper_description.md to learn Income is a median split and Newspaper has 2 levels. Notes that the chi-squared test of independence is symmetric in var1/var2 — picks var1='Income', var2='Newspaper' as a sensible convention. Fits with rsm.basics.cross_tabs({'newspaper': df}, var1='Income', var2='Newspaper'), prints summary(output=['observed','expected','chisq','dev_std']), and walks through: H0 (no association) and Ha (association) in plain English; the observed table (Low Income: 83 WSJ, 276 USA Today; High Income: 180 WSJ, 41 USA Today); the expected table under independence (Low: 162.8/196.2, High: 100.2/120.8); the chi-sq contribution table (all cells contribute substantially, total chi-sq=187.78); the dev_std table (Low Income WSJ: -6.25, Low Income USA Today: +5.70, High Income WSJ: +7.97, High Income USA Today: -7.26 — all far beyond 1.96 in absolute value). Checks the expected-cell-count assumption from the footer (0% of cells below 5 — assumption fully satisfied). States verdict: chi-sq=187.78 on 1 df, p<.001, critical chi-sq at alpha=0.05 (df=1) is 3.841 — reject H0. Most importantly, unpacks the dev_std table to tell the substantive story: 'High-income readers are strongly over-represented among WSJ readers and under-represented among USA Today readers; the low-income pattern mirrors it. Reach high-income readers via WSJ; reach low-income via USA Today.' Optionally suggests using ct.summary(output=['perc_row']) for a marketing-style 'what fraction of each income segment reads each paper' view.

evals.prompt: Same newspaper data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/newspaper.parquet. Can you also show me the full diagnostic suite (observed, expected, chisq, dev_std, perc_row, perc_col) and explain which cells drive the rejection and which percentage-table is the right one for a marketing decision?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: refits the same cross_tab and prints summary(output=['observed','expected','chisq','dev_std','perc_row','perc_col']). Walks through each table in order, then explicitly addresses the percentage question: (a) perc_row answers 'given an income level, what fraction reads each paper?' — useful for a marketing decision of 'how do I reach low-income readers' (answer: ~77% read USA Today); (b) perc_col answers 'given a paper, what fraction of readers are each income?' — useful for an ad-buyer asking 'who reads WSJ' (answer: ~68% high-income); (c) the row-vs-column distinction is the substantive question, not a statistical one. For the chi-sq cell drivers, uses the chisq contribution table: each cell contributes 32-64 to the omnibus 187.78; high-income WSJ contributes the most (63.5). Confirms via dev_std: |dev_std| > 5 in every cell, with high-income WSJ at +7.97 the largest single deviation. Multi-comparison caveat: with R*C = 4 cells, a strict per-cell Bonferroni threshold would be |dev_std| > 1.96 + correction ≈ 2.50, still survived by all four. Recommends final reporting language: 'High-income readers are over-represented as WSJ readers (observed 180 vs expected 100, dev_std +7.97) and under-represented as USA Today readers (41 vs 121, dev_std -7.26); ~81% of high-income readers chose WSJ versus ~23% of low-income readers.'

evals.prompt: Test if Income and Newspaper are associated in ~/Downloads/newspaper.parquet.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I ran the cross_tab on the newspaper data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/newspaper.parquet and got chi-squared = 187.78 with p < .001. So Income and Newspaper are strongly associated — done. Can I write that up?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) acknowledges that yes, the omnibus rejection is solid (chi-sq=187.78 on 1 df ≫ critical 3.841, p < .001), but pushes back on STOPPING there as the complete writeup; (2) explains the central pedagogical point: the omnibus chi-squared says 'somewhere in this joint distribution is a deviation from independence'; it does NOT say WHERE or BY HOW MUCH; (3) STRONGLY recommends running summary with output=['dev_std'] (or the full diagnostic suite) before writing up — the standardized-deviation table is what turns 'associated' into a substantive story; (4) walks through what dev_std reveals for this dataset: all 4 cells exceed |dev_std| > 5, with high-income WSJ at +7.97 (over-represented) and low-income WSJ at -6.25 (under-represented); the mirror pattern in USA Today (5.70, -7.26); (5) reframes the writeup to include the dev_std interpretation: 'income and newspaper choice are strongly associated (chi-sq=187.78, df=1, p<.001). The association is driven by all four cells: high-income readers are over-represented among WSJ readers (observed 180 vs expected 100, dev_std +7.97) and correspondingly under-represented among USA Today readers (41 vs 121, dev_std -7.26).' (6) also reminds the user to: (a) note the expected-count assumption check (0% below 5 — clean), (b) report percentages (perc_row or perc_col depending on the audience), (c) avoid causal language — cross_tabs is symmetric and shows association, not causation; (7) optionally mentions that for a 2x2 table the dev_std story is symmetric (one cell dictates all four arithmetically), but for larger R x C tables the dev_std table is essential for identifying WHICH cells drive the rejection.
